title: Let's Exchange Ideas and Share your AI gamedev workflow, what's actually working for you right now?
author: Any_Inevitable_4035
selftext:
Seeing a lot of different setups here lately, so I thought it'd be useful to collect them in one place.

If you're making games with AI, what does your workflow look like?

* What engine are you using?
* Which tools for code, art, and sound?
* How do you keep the AI on track on bigger features?
* What's one tip you wish you'd known earlier?

Even small setups help. Someone just starting out will probably learn more from your messy real workflow than from any tutorial.

I'll add mine in the comments.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Unreal engine 5 
Claude, codex, Gemini and Operncode for API. 
I build a watcher, he manages CPU and GPU usage while keeping an eye on all running agents. Usually 1 ue agent and 3-4 coding agents. Running most of the time for the 24h day. 
Claude is the orchestrator and delegates packages to other clients. A haiku watchdog is supporting my watcher tool. 

And for the ones asking why: emergent full medieval simulation from settlers to thriving city with castles. At the moment 64*64km² while stimulating every single citizen with needs. Think anno but bigger and more realistic with real castles and forts that grow organically. 

I decide everything, while at the PC we go and plan every system and build every visible aspect. At night everything that I don't see happens

With this setup I'm using every model to its strengths and saving a lot of tokens. Vibecoding for 12h but only spent about 5% Claude (200$) 4% codex (100$)  and full 5h limit of Gemini (23$)

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: A 64x64 km sim with every citizen having needs is wild. How's performance holding up at that scale? And I love the split of planning together by day and letting the agents run overnight. Do you review everything they did each morning, or trust the watcher to flag issues?

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
Yes of cause I review the results but I ve to trust the watcher. My development style is very strict. Ai agents only have rights to one specific thing. 

Regarding the simulation. Unreal really helps with the huge map, awesome graphics and without nanite it would be way harder. Just the 280 million trees were a problem but after culling and some more optimisation I basically have 4 seasons with dynamic leafs with weather and everything with 60fps. But I didn't scale the simulation yet. That's what I am working on right now. 

And you simply can't calculate a live simulation for the environment and all the NPC agents while performing 60fps in UE. 

And all that combined with a fast forward feature, real-time, 2x, 5x, 10x, 100x
The 100x is the real problem for a simulation. 


I only add features to my main branch that still guarantee minimum 60 FPS in the dev build. I would love more but my CPU is crappy.

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: 280 million trees at 60fps on a crappy CPU is impressive lol. The 60fps gate on the main branch is a great rule too, it's probably what keeps the overnight agents from quietly tanking performance. Good luck scaling the sim, would love to see it once citizens are running at that size.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: Well I would have 280 million. But on the whole 4000km² combined. I only show about 2km². Everything else is to far away, you couldn't see the individual tree.

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035

comments.author: Such--Balance
comments.body:
I went in deep on my first game project. Not make an easy game first. Just start building what i actually want to build.

Does it work? Im not sure. All the pitfalls of starting to big are there. Its spagetti already and im kinda losing oversight.

I am learning a lot though. Mostly from what not to do. If theres ever gonna be a second game i can incorperate all those lessons.

Overall though, ai is so good that it can work around or patch most serious problems (so far)

I just made a test environment for navigation and pathfinding. For a top down 2d open map tower defense game. It was struggling with 150+ enemies.

The test environment could handle 30k in way larger maps. Just migrated large parts over to my main game which can now hold 15k+ enemies with instant repathing when walls or terrain changes.

Ai is batshit crazy man. Still took a lot of actual work and finetuning but its crazy man. 100x gains on movement and pathfinding

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: 150 to 15k enemies with instant repathing is insane, nice work. Building a separate test environment first was a smart call too. Are you doing flow fields for that? And what engine is it in? Curious how you're handling the spaghetti part, I hit that early too.

replies.author: Such--Balance
replies.body:
Yeah its flowfields. Migrated to c++ as well. Im working in Godot. I have zero c++ experience. But now with ai might as well migrate whats just way more efficient to do in c++.

Yeah the spagetti is a problem. Its a lack of general knowledge, the general setup of the project and just getting used to everything and learning at the same time.

Im willing to bet this is just somewhat part of the reality regardless though. Theres always more ideas than implementations and always more implementations that what you eventually need.

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body:
\> What engine are you using?  
Plain C! But I'm mostly making ROMs GBA games.

\> Which tools for code, art, and sound?  
Sprite Fusion for anything pixel art (sprites, animations...), my own virtual synth for anything SFX and music.

\> How do you keep the AI on track on bigger features?  
I Babysit it, there no real hack here. Also I ask the LLM to always make comparisons etc.

\> What's one tip you wish you'd known earlier?  
Art Direction is very, very important. LLMs are averaging machines, to escape that you need to pull great inspirations from everywhere (design, hardware, films etc)

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: GBA ROMs in plain C is such a cool niche. "LLMs are averaging machines" is a great way to put it, and it's true for code too, not just art. What does asking it to make comparisons look like in practice? Do you have it lay out a couple of approaches before it writes anything?

replies.author: HugoDzz
replies.body: 100% agree on code quality yeah! For comparisons, it is all HTML-based, I love working with a style-frame canvas/ideation board. But it's specific for me I guess, other people might prefer other ways!

comments.author: TheVoyant
comments.body:
Custom C++ 20/Typescript engine,
Massively opened things up because all the code the Ai could understand and use.

I built a full devkit, the tools to make the games as standalone modules that plug into each other. Game creates receiver lightweight versions that plug it into live. 

First month or two was exhausting almost gave up, biggest hurdle was Claude, it was slow and unreliable/inventing problems. Switched off into hybrid sub/api stack with custom harness tailored to the devtools, plugged in the CLIs from Codex and Antigravity. Astra for visual work; Neon/Carbon for everything else, using Mimo as my cheap compute if needed. 

Making the tools was rough but now that I have them, custom vfx, animations, lighting, 3D modelling, etc is all designed how my brain understands, so the friction is non-existent. I used keywords for everything, so when I have a random thought I can "vibecode" and because the engine is written in my own vocabulary the Ai has a direct path to the knowledge.

Also developing a very structured review process, pre checks, and brain/memory systems (look into engines for cortex simulation and hermes agent's method) helped immensely.

From there its compartmentalized so theres an agent specialized for every module so even as a sub agent they can be called and ready/primed with all context.

More setup for greater ease of use/development later.

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: Writing the engine in your own vocabulary so the AI has a direct path to it is a really smart idea, I haven't seen anyone frame it like that. Having an agent primed for each module sounds like it'd solve most of the context-drift problems people mention here. How long did the devkit take before it started paying off?

replies.author: TheVoyant
replies.body: Month 3, granted I had no understanding of anything I was doing yet. Made probably every mistake along the way lol.

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: Ha, month 3 from zero understanding to a full custom engine is still really fast. Making every mistake is probably why it works so well now. Good luck with it!

replies.author: TheVoyant
replies.body:
100%.
Failure is the path to success. 

Godspeed and gl!

comments.author: SweetKarmaz
comments.body:
I am using Claude Code with Unity for my first real game, Kinhold. But I have also been building my own engine that I will use for the next game after. Right now, I use AI only for code and initial art, and as I get features complete I then use purchased art assets. I have tried using all the AI art tricks, and none work to my satisfaction. After about 8 months, I have learned a lot about what works for me. I create game bibles for everything! For Kinhold, everything gets its own bible - the four big ones are how the Kinfolk systems interact, how resources work and what they are for, all the recipes and the requirements, and code. Any time a script is updated, the code bible gets a changelog. Every other month, I run a code audit to remove redundant and outdated code, and a check on changes that can improve game performance. The final thing everyone should do, is have other people playtest your game - its one thing to have AI playtest it, but its another to have real people. Dont tell them how the game is supposed to work, have them figure it out on their own. It is always hard finding playtesters if you dont know anyone personally, though, but it is possible.

And now after 8 months, I am close to releasing a real game on Steam! Never thought I would get to this point.

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: Congrats on getting close to a Steam release, 8 months from first game to that is huge. The game bible with a changelog for every script update is a great habit, I'm stealing that. Is Kinhold's Steam page up yet? Would love to wishlist it. Unity also has other AI free assistants which can help you with context switching

replies.author: SweetKarmaz
replies.body: Steam page and the game build are in review right now, so soon I hope! I have a website that goes into that, and a bit of the second game I am in the planning stages on (https://sweetkarmazstudios.com/), but it doesnt have any updates since October 1st - It has been two months of improving the world and replacing art assets and fine tuning, including a real game trailer. Once I get the steam page approved, I will update my website as well.

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: for my browser game i use Codex and Claude Code. i describe the player action i want, then check it in the game after each change. i also keep player feedback and bugs as separate lists. a feature can work in code and still feel bad when someone plays it. watching where real players leave has helped me more than asking the AI if the feature is finished.

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: "A feature can work in code and still feel bad" is so true, and the AI will always tell you it's finished lol. Keeping feedback and bugs as separate lists is smart too. How do you track where players leave, analytics or just watching people play?

comments.author: chapeaubas92
comments.body:
I'm using my own engine i made with claude and three.js.  
Upgraded claude with some skill that let him be a artist :-).

  
For code , claude , for the art also claude and sound i use elevenlabs

I have made a todo list that has so far 500+ tasks to do, and we go through them step for step.  
Everything is organized!

My own tip for myself if i started earlier, don't be afraid to put a whole novel with something you have in your head in the chat.  
I've been doing small steps untill i noticed i had a great idea of a game that i would want to make with everything in it that I liked.  
I was busy writing it down for like a hour and pressed enter, it took claude some time to make a whole concept from it.  
And 2 months later we're still building on it! Slowly and steady i've managed to make something i'm proud off.

https://i.redd.it/uyc1v3fcb54i1.png

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: That screenshot looks great, the water arena with the glowing runes is really nice for a custom three.js engine. And I like the "write the whole novel" tip, that's the opposite of what most people here say, but it makes sense once you know what you want. Is "The Lock Warden" a boss fight?

comments.author: lorean_victor
comments.body:
depends on the project.

one is basically normal godot + pixelorama for art + garage band for music. codex has readonly access to files and guides me.

another one is a web based rts, so codex has full control. no setup or anything.

I also constantly churn out mini vibes based on random ideas i have, and share them on a feed i built with a friend with a bunch of other players / creators. the app has nice mcps with guidelines and tools for storage or basic sfx or previews, so i just use its codex mcp (if anyone is interested you can check it out on https://vibed.city)

replies.author: Any_Inevitable_4035
replies.body: Interesting split, read-only access for the Godot project but full control on the web RTS. Makes sense depending on how much you want to learn vs. just ship. [Vibed.city](http://Vibed.city) sounds fun, what kinds of mini games are people sharing there?

replies.author: lorean_victor
replies.body:
typically really tiny experiences. some are addictive, but most are kind of “consumable”, it’s a fun idea, you play a few times, and you move on.

ofc there’s “remixing” so a lot of stuff are also just variation on other ideas and “vibes”.

comments.author: Hotwingz66
comments.body:
Godot

Gpt image but trying to find a way to replace it

I have a mission statement does and donts.
One feature at a time. No tolerance for Red or yellow errors.

No tips to give. Yea you can read about md files skills etc etc. But I prefer to solve one problem at a time, if I need a new tool, Ill figure out how to make it. Nothing beats figuring out what you need when you need it. 

Or you end up setting up a very sophisticated system you dont understand or dont need.


One small tip ill share is, if you figure out a process. Take some time to have your llm evaluate the process and then turn that into a new skill.

comments.author: starmakereden

I use ChatGPT to expand on my idea and brainstormed with it to create design rules, frameworks, systems, etc. Used Godot MCP, Blender MCP, Photoshop MCP.

  
My workflow normally goes like this: tell chatgpt what feature I want to build, they give me a codex prompt, review and check for any bugs, do the whole process again. Honestly, I mostly use AI to help implement the code. I have generated concept art as a reference to build a feature but that's it.

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body:
I'm still at the stage where my workflow is different for every project. Right now I have two works in progress: one is using Superpowers, the other is more vibey. Both are built for the browser on Phaser, primarily using Claude Code with some custom skills.

At this point I have them both pretty close to functionally complete, but I'm starting to run into the limitations of what coding agents can do for me: AI is great for accelerating programming, but I still have no (usable) graphics, sound, playtesters, or marketing. And there's no point releasing without those.
